source.title: Alexa Teacher Model: Pretraining and Distilling Multi-Billion-Parameter Encoders for Natural Language Understanding Systems
source.citation: Jack G. M. FitzGerald et al., 2022

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out perplexity at two encoder sizes and reports downstream XNLI accuracy across model sizes. This is a different setup from fitting and testing the original scaling laws, and it does not fit a power law.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out no-fine-tune perplexity for two AlexaTM sizes and says perplexity correlates strongly with XNLI accuracy across updates. It cites scaling-law work in Related Work, but cited results are not extracted. Other results on NLU, distillation, and full-system performance do not measure the claim’s scaling-law quantities. The Table 3 XLM-R Large perplexity comparison is not included as a size-scaling result because it is a single comparator trained on written-form data.
record.test_reason: This is a production NLU pipeline paper. It cites Kaplan et al. only in Related Work and fits no scaling law. Its only size-related numbers are incidental and cannot show any version's effect. Held-out MLM perplexity is reported for just two Stage 1 encoders (2.3B, 9.3B; about 4x apart). These two runs differ in batch tokens (1M vs 2M), warmup, schedule and max length (Table 7), so neither a power-law form nor the absence of other bottlenecks can be read. XNLI accuracy exists for only two pretrained sizes, which cannot show whether improvement is predictable. The perplexity–XNLI correlation is within one 2.3B run across update steps and is shown only as a figure. The reader's 'tests'/T2 overstates this; the size comparisons are descriptive, not a test of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that a large teacher, Stage 2 in-domain pretraining, teacher-assistant distillation and in-domain final distillation are key to improving NLU and full-system results. They make no scaling-law claims beyond noting that perplexity falls with size, as expected.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains multilingual masked-language-model encoders on spoken-form and written-form mixtures, reports perplexity for two sizes, and does not fit or extrapolate scaling laws or optimize a fixed compute budget.
record.method_sensitivity: Training stage and distillation status differ across some of the XNLI model-size comparisons; the paper also describes spoken-form versus written-form data, but does not report a controlled comparison of these choices for the scaling results.

fits_no_version.finding: Within one 2.3B run, perplexity and noun mask-filling accuracy correlate strongly with XNLI accuracy across update steps (figure only). The purpose is choosing a no-fine-tune validation metric.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Held-out MLM perplexity tracks downstream accuracy over training steps within a single model.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing a fine-tuned, distilled final model from 5M to 17M parameters, otherwise equal, improved offline SemER by only 0.25–0.38%. Separately, a 170M Stage 2 student matched its 2.3B teacher on in-domain NLU, and the authors suggest the teacher may be overparameterized for the task.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For production NLU distillation, final student size yields small gains relative to teacher pretraining and domain data.

record.peer_reviewed: KDD ’22, Proceedings of the 28th ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
record.problems: The relevant perplexity comparison contains only two sizes and no uncertainty estimates or power-law fit. XNLI accuracy comparisons involving the 170M model are confounded by distillation; the stated perplexity–XNLI correlation is described as strong but is not numerically reported in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 also reports XNLI scores for XLM-R and mT5 model families; these public-model comparisons are omitted because they do not provide controlled AlexaTM scaling or paired held-out-loss measurements. Table 3's XLM-R Large perplexity comparator is omitted because it is a single model trained on written-form data, rather than a size-scaling datapoint.

untested.parts: Power-law form, exponents, several orders of magnitude, token and compute axes. Only two uncontrolled perplexity points exist.
All; no extrapolation from small runs.
All; no shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
All; Stage 2 and spoken-form training have no scaling analysis.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or loss across sizes. Only two pretrained sizes, plus a within-run correlation.
All; no fitting choices are compared.

missing.what: Noun mask-filling accuracy by size (62.74 for 2.3B vs 65.09 for 9.3B, spoken-form data).
Training-setup differences between the 2.3B and 9.3B teachers (batch tokens 1M vs 2M, warmup, LR, max length), which confound any size comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Kaplan et al. appears only in Related Work. The reader's V1/V6 'supports' labels rest on two uncontrolled points and the distillation-confounded comparison; they are withdrawn. Rows R1–R2 and R18–R24 are kept linked so researchers can see the raw size comparisons, but they are marked cannot_determine.

versions.untested_parts: Only no-fine-tune perplexity for the 2.3B and 9.3B Stage 1 models is reported; there is no power-law fit, exponent, test over several orders of magnitude, or sweep over tokens or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict the loss of larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token scaling is reported.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count is reported.
The study includes spoken-form data and Stage 2 in-domain pretraining, but does not test whether the same power-law loss form holds across these or other training regimes.

The study reports XNLI accuracy across model sizes and a stated perplexity–XNLI correlation across updates, but does not establish a general downstream prediction rule or test other downstream task families.
The study does not compare fitting choices or exponents, or argue from its own results that scaling curves bend or depend on such choices.

rows.subject: AlexaTM 2.3B Stage 1
rows.operation_detail: Measured no-fine-tune perplexity on spoken-form data.
rows.note: One of the two AlexaTM sizes with reported perplexity; the paper expects perplexity to decrease with increasing model size.
rows.check: A single perplexity point cannot show a power law. It is the baseline for R2, not an effect in itself.

rows.subject: AlexaTM 9.3B Stage 1
rows.operation_detail: Measured no-fine-tune perplexity on spoken-form data.
rows.note: Perplexity is lower than for the 2.3B model, but these two points do not establish a power-law form.
rows.check: Two points 4x apart in size, with different batch tokens, schedules and max lengths (Table 7). The drop 11.56→8.80 is in the expected direction, but the measure cannot show the power-law form over orders of magnitude, so 'observed' overstates it.

rows.check: Figure-only correlation across update steps of one 2.3B model, with no value given. It is about validation-metric choice, not scale. It does not show downstream performance predicted by loss across scale.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: AlexaTM Stage 1 models evaluated on spoken-form data
reader_labels.reason: Perplexity is lower for the 9.3B than the 2.3B model (R1–R2), consistent with a decline as size increases, although this does not test the power-law shape.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Only two model sizes are measured, with no fitted exponent or evidence for a power law over several orders of magnitude (R1–R2).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The 9.3B model has higher accuracy than the 2.3B Stage 1 model in English, the reported zero-shot average, and each listed non-English language; the study also states that perplexity correlates strongly with XNLI accuracy across updates (R3, R18–R24).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Comparison of distilled 170M and 2.3B Stage 1 XNLI models
reader_labels.reason: The larger model scores higher across the reported languages, but the 170M model is distilled, so the comparison does not isolate parameter count alone (R4–R17).
